#4647. 1,500 years ago, a man trekked across Europe as the Roman Empire fell

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:56 AM EST

If you were going to live in Europe at any point in time, word of advice: Avoid the fifth century. The mighty Roman Empire was floundering. Attila the Hun repeatedly invaded the eastern Roman Empire, and even Italy in the year 452 CE. Fierce Germanic forces known as the Visigoths and Vandals sacked and raided Rome, first in 410 and again in 455. The Franks (in present-day France, Belgium, and western Germany) were busy wresting control in the west. And in 476, the entire Roman Empire collapsed. Put simply, it was a rough century.

With all of that upheaval, many people picked up and left their homes, undoubtedly in search of better, more stable places to live. Historians call the period between the fourth and seventh centuries in Europe as the Migration Period since so many people were on the move.

Now, thanks to some 1,500-year-old DNA from an elaborate ship burial in northwestern Germany, we are tantalizingly close to understanding one man’s journey from one end of the Roman Empire to the other. Oh, and he also had leprosy.

This grueling, potentially 800-mile-long journey is detailed in a study published in this month’s edition of the journal iScience.

Discovered in the 1990s, the Fallward burial ground is a treasure trove of information from the Migration Period. Located on coastal marshland, about 20 miles west of Hamburg, Germany, the cemetery contains about 200 cremation burials and 60 graves from the end of the third to the late fifth century. Many of the graves were dug deep into damp clay, which has helped preserve many striking finds.

One of the most remarkable graves is simply labeled as site 265. The grave belongs to an approximately 50-year-old man, who died sometime between 425 and 450. The man probably rowed or fished along the German coast since his skeletal remains indicate his upper arm muscles were well developed. He was also buried inside a 13-foot-long oak boat covered with wooden panels that formed a roof-like structure.

But the boat burial isn’t the only thing that makes grave 265 unique.

“The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest; these included a chair, artfully decorated and carved from an alder trunk. Furthermore, the man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances,” explained Dr. Hauke Jöns from the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research in Wilhelmshaven, Germany, explained in a statement on the new findings.

The elaborate chair was presumably painted and is often referred to as a throne. Far from an ordinary piece of furniture meant for daily use, it was instead a symbol of the authority the deceased wielded in life.

The late Roman military belt perhaps raises the most questions about who the man buried in 265 was. The belt shows signs of both use and repair. While its presence doesn’t necessarily mean the man was a soldier in the Roman military—he could’ve acquired it through trade, inheritance, or as war booty—it also doesn’t mean he wasn’t a soldier for Rome. If he was, he would have likely been part of the foederati. These warriors served Rome through a treaty, or foedus, rather than as Roman citizens.

The grave also included: a stool carved with a hunting scene and inscription, a game board, a ceramic vessel, and a bronze basin.

For nearly 30 years, archaeologists could only speculate about what these grave goods meant about who was buried in grave 265. But with the new DNA analysis, we now have some concrete answers about who this man was. Though the team was able to extract DNA from three individuals from the Fallward burial ground, “the results were particularly striking” for the man in 265. The new genetic analysis confirms two things about the man.

First, he was from or had close family from the Danube region in the eastern part of the Roman Empire, which comprised parts of modern day Croatia, Hungary, Slovenia, and Serbia. That’s a long way from his grave in northwestern Germany, so at some point he or a close relative traveled more than 800 miles, leaving behind the Roman Empire in process. Second, he had a rare form of leprosy.

“Leprosy is a chronic disease. It can take years for clear symptoms to appear. The man had not yet suffered any bone damage. Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease,” explained study co-author Dr. Almut Nebel from the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Christian-Albrechts-University in Kiel, Germany.

Study co-author Dr. Ben Krause-Kyora (also at IKMB) speculates, “He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers, which run on either side of Fallward]. Or he might have undertaken long journeys as a trader.”

Either way, the man in grave 265 likely lived through a heck of a lot before taking up fishing on the rural German coastline.

#4646. Learning Emotion Regulation... From a Horse?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Strong human emotions are often difficult to manage, and learning to control them is never easy. Most skeptics would assume that no animal, let alone a horse, could help us humans develop emotion regulation… but they can.

Unlike humans, with our over-reliance on vision, horses navigate the world primarily through smell and touch. The average horse has all the neurological machinery to detect and interpret odors that a bloodhound has. Bloodhounds, just for reference, can detect an odor that’s 12 days old from 12 miles away. Not bad, given that we humans can barely sniff out raw steak on the kitchen counter.

The average horse also has exquisite touch sensitivity. Many areas of her skin can detect a lighter touch than the human fingertip is capable of feeling. She can sense a rider turn his head a couple inches to the left or right, even when he’s invisible up in the saddle. She notices the slightest touch of a single finger on her reins and the barest pressure of the rider’s legs against her sides. The weights and pressures horses can detect often exceed human capacity.

OK, so horses are cool. But what do these sharpened senses have to do with emotional regulation? Everything. Horses are emotional mirrors. They pick up human emotions instantly using smell and touch, then reflect them to the human rider or handler through equine body language. Remember, horses are herd animals, accustomed to reading the slightest nuances from their companions.

Let’s suppose you’re travelling along one day on a horse you ride often. Gator notices through feel that your muscles are more tense than usual, your joints feel stiff, and you aren’t quite as forgiving with your hands. His prey brain tells him maybe something is wrong. Now, a prey animal like a horse can’t afford to ponder your tension; to survive a potential predatory chase, he has to run now. Maybe you have sensed some danger that he doesn’t know about yet, and using good herd behavior, Gator doesn’t want to wait around and find out.

So… he becomes tense, stiff, and less forgiving. His head shoots up, his ears prick forward, his mouth hardens, and his nostrils open wide to sniff the air for danger. His muscles turn from butter to concrete. He is mirroring your nervousness with anxiety of his own, and sitting astride a 1,200-pound animal that’s seven or eight feet long, you will feel his anxiety immediately.

As a rider, you can’t afford to allow Gator to maintain that high level of anxiety. Soon, he will explode in fear—bolting, spinning, bucking—and you will hit the dirt, likely breaking a few bones in the process. That’s why horses and riders have to notice each other’s emotions.

It also explains why we have to regulate our human emotions when working with horses, whose brains are driven primarily by fear even under the best circumstances. To accommodate that physiology, the rider or handler must remain relaxed. So, much of learning to ride a horse is learning to manage our human emotions. When we aren’t sure what we feel (nervous? scared? weak? fluttery?), our horses tell us.

Sometimes while riding, I notice that a horse is nervous and wonder why. It could be his temperament, background, former training, feed, the weather, deer in the distance, or any number of things. But often it’s because I’m nervous about something and don’t know it. Perhaps business responsibilities concern me, maybe a frenemy just drove in, or sometimes I’m in a hurry to make my next appointment or make a call to offset the latest family drama. Any of these situations can cause nervous human tension, anger, or frustration, all of which the horse can feel.

Horses tell us with their bodies that our human tension exists, and they show us how it feels. To calm a horse, we have no choice but to calm ourselves. We breathe deeply and loud enough that the horse hears us (for he will also mirror our breath), we train our muscles to relax even when we’re worried, we lower our shoulders and soften our necks, and we allow our bodies to move more fluidly to match the horse’s normal movement.

Do that every day with a huge, powerful animal, and… yep, you will learn to regulate your emotions. From a horse!

#4645. BYD’s new luxury electric SUV has one big problem: It weighs over 8,200 lbs

BYD’s new full-size electric SUV, the Denza N9 EV, was revealed in a regulatory filing, weighing in at over 8,200 lbs (3,760 kg). That creates one issue.

The Denza N9 first went on sale last March, a flagship plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV with a combined CLTC range of about 807 miles (1,300 km) on a full charge and full tank of gas.

BYD introduced the updated Flash Charging version earlier this year, which uses its second-generation Blade Batteries and delivers a pure electric CLTC range of 260 miles (420 km). Combined, it gets up to 944 miles (1,520 km) under CLTC conditions.

In the latest batch of new energy vehicles (NEVs) approved for sale by China’s MIIT (Ministry of Information Technology) this week, a new all-electric Denza N9 appeared.

The filing revealed the Denza N9 EV will be available with three electric motors, delivering a combined output of 1,193 horsepower (890 kW).

A badge on the back reveals it will use BYD’s tri-motor e3 platform. The setup features a single 362 horsepower (270 kW) front motor and two 415 horsepower (310 kW) rear electric motors.

The electric version measures 5,270 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,830 mm tall, with a 3,125 mm wheelbase, which is the same as the current Denza N9 PHEV Flash Charging model. It will be available in five- and six-seat configurations.

While the filing reveals it will use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with cells from BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, it does not provide specifics like capacity or driving range.

One relatively big thing to note: the Denza N9 EV has a gross weight of 3,760 kg, or about 8,289 lbs.

Obscene weight , and that applies to other SUVs as well. Vehicle registration taxes should be based on vehicle weight as it wears out roads and endangers other road users and infrastructure and wastes resources.

As AutoNext points out, this makes it too heavy for an EU category B driving license, which covers up to 3,500 kg (7,716 lbs).

Last year, the EU updated the rules, allowing drivers who have held a category B license for two years to drive alternative-fuelled vehicles with a maximum weight of up to 4,250 kg (9,369 lbs).

While the Denza N9 EV would qualify as listed, newer drivers would still need a commercial EU category C1 driving license to drive it.

BYD launched its luxury sub-brand, Denza, in Europe and the UK in March, starting with the Z9 GT and the D9 van. More recently, it introduced the Bao 5 PHEV SUV and the Denza Z electric supercar.

#4643. Why Trying to Control People Often Backfires

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

The holidays have a way of resurfacing family conflict. Whether we’re arguing about politics, religion, or putting pineapple on pizza, telling someone what to think rarely changes their mind. In fact, it typically makes them fight back harder. I’ve witnessed this reaction as a father, physician, White House adviser, and public health advocate—especially when disease outbreaks erode public trust.

During the pandemic, public health mandates seemed to intensify suspicions among people who were already skeptical of the government and vaccines. Americans adopted an "us-versus-them" mentality and stopped listening to anyone with an opposing view.

Scientists have a name for this: psychological reactance—the tendency to push back against restrictions that interfere with our freedom. Even when rules are meant to keep us safe, we resist because we don’t want someone else making decisions for us.

The sense that our autonomy is under threat dampens activity in the brain’s prefrontal cortex, which is involved in reasoning and synthesizing new information. This reduces our openness to evidence and explains why relying solely on control tends to backfire.

Curiosity, on the other hand, engages the brain's learning and reward systems. When we are invited to explore the benefits and risks of a decision, rather than being told what to think, the brain’s prefrontal cortex activity is enhanced and we become more open to considering new information. Our brains become primed to learn, making uptake of behavior more likely.

Put another way, while pressure engages threat circuits, curiosity engages learning circuits in our brains. That’s important because while control may push people to comply, it doesn’t establish the trust required to build lasting change.

During the pandemic, my Rishi Uncle was furious about government restrictions that had forced his motel business to shut down. He distrusted the government and listened to political commentators whose views were very different from mine.

As a physician working to protect people against COVID, I found his position deeply frustrating. I wanted him to understand the science and recognize the danger the virus posed to him and his family.

But I was so frightened that I didn't have the conversation I needed to have with him. My father did.

Rather than trying to change Rishi Uncle's beliefs, my father approached him with curiosity. As I listened to them speak, I started learning more about my uncle’s perspective. He watched as loved ones fell ill and died, feeling helpless. As a business owner, his livelihood was also under serious threat.

Despite his anger toward the government, my uncle wore a mask when he left the house and eventually got vaccinated. He recognized the risks facing himself and his family and made choices to protect them. He didn't have to change all his political beliefs to change his behavior.

Looking back, I wish I'd spent less time feeling frustrated with my uncle and more time trying to understand him. People may disagree about politics or personal freedoms, but they can often find common ground in protecting the ones they love.

Every tough conversation doesn’t end with a resolution, but it also doesn’t have to end with a blowout fight. While working with patients and communities, I’ve developed a few approaches to navigate disagreement in a healthier and more productive way.

Resist the urge to immediately correct someone when they say something you disagree with. Instead, ask them to identify their biggest concern: "What worries you most about this?"

Understanding the story behind someone’s beliefs and fears provides the context you need to address their concerns without alienating them in the process.

In the same vein, explaining how your own experiences have shaped your opinion can help someone see your point of view. Personal stories help people feel seen and heard and create opportunities to find common ground, shared experiences, and values, even if your opinions conflict.

Remember, you don’t have to change someone’s beliefs to change their behaviors. Someone who distrusts the government may still choose to get vaccinated to protect their family. A driver who thinks the speed limit is too low may still slow down to keep neighborhood children safe.

Try identifying the values you share—like protecting your family and friends—instead of demanding they agree with every issue.

In late 2023, I spoke at a symposium organized by Boston University and Harvard Medical School about lessons learned during the COVID pandemic. My panel focused on how to communicate important health information and counter misinformation.

That’s when I had a thought: Are we spending too much time trying to figure out why people are not listening to public health experts and not enough time listening to what they have to say?

This is one of the most important questions we can ask ourselves when we’re in a disagreement. It helps us shift from control to curiosity, accepting we may be wrong, listening to someone else’s perspective, and being open to a conversation that doesn’t end with a "winner."

Trust grows only when we’re willing to listen to each other. So, next time you’re frustrated that someone isn’t listening to you, consider how much you’ve done to try to understand them.

Steindl, C., Jonas, E., Sittenthaler, S., Traut-Mattausch, E., & Greenberg, J. (2015). Understanding psychological reactance: New developments and findings. Zeitschrift für Psychologie, 223(4), 205–214. https://doi.org/10.1027/2151-2604/a000222

Panjabi, R. (2026). Safer: A playbook—turning fear into action and crisis into community. HarperOne.

#4642. Germany’s EV share hits record 37% as BEVs beat gas and diesel combined

Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.

For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.

The overall market barely grew in October. Total new car registrations rose 1.7% to 254,492 units, which means the EV growth came straight out of combustion cars.

Gasoline car registrations crashed 40.5% to 38,516 units, a 15.1% share. Diesel fell 21.6% to 23,882 units, or 9.4% of the market. Add them up and pure combustion cars made up just 24.5% of new registrations, 12.5 points less than BEVs alone.

Plug-in hybrids slipped 7.9% to 28,499 units (11.2%). So plug-ins accounted for about 48% of the German market last month, and the average CO2 emissions of new cars dropped 21.1% year-over-year to 79.4 g/km.

As we reported this summer, BEVs became the most popular powertrain in Germany for the first time in June with a 28.4% share. They’ve kept climbing every month since: 32.4% in August, 34.5% in September, and now 37% in October.

Through the first ten months of the year, Germany has registered 698,230 BEVs, up 60.7% year-over-year. That’s about 28.2% of the 2,476,290 new cars registered in 2026 so far, up from roughly 19% for the full year 2025.

And the industry didn’t see it coming. In December, the VDA, Germany’s auto industry association, forecast about 693,000 BEV registrations for all of 2026. Germany passed that in October. At the current pace, it’s on track for somewhere around 875,000 by the end of the year.

The biggest driver is Germany’s new EV incentive, which applies retroactively to cars registered since January 1. It pays €3,000 for a new BEV, bought or leased, and up to €6,000 for lower-income households with children. Households with taxable income above €80,000 (€90,000 with kids) don’t qualify.

The program targets private buyers, and that’s exactly where the KBA data shows the jump. Private registrations rose 20.6% in October, while commercial registrations fell 8.2%. Private buyers now make up 40.7% of the market.

Germany has been here before. The government killed its previous EV incentive overnight in December 2023, and BEV sales fell off a cliff in 2024. This time, the money is going to the buyers who need it most, and it’s moving the needle fast.

Tesla’s German numbers swing wildly with its quarterly delivery cycle. In September, the end of the quarter, it registered 12,552 cars (+268.7%) and the Model Y was the best-selling car in Germany. In October, it registered only 2,932, which is still up 290.9% but from a tiny base, for a 1.2% market share.

Year-to-date, Tesla is up 206.1% to 47,742 registrations. That’s a big rebound from a terrible 2025, but BYD is now slightly ahead with 47,961 (+216.1%). BYD registered 5,173 cars in October (+54.3%), though the majority of its German sales are plug-in hybrids, not BEVs.

The other Chinese brands are growing even faster. Leapmotor registered 3,661 cars in October, up 288.6%, and is at 19,705 for the year. Xpeng was up 284.4% to 1,380 units, and SAIC’s MG was up 48.5% to 4,140.

Volkswagen Group still owns the top of the EV charts, though. Through September, the Skoda Elroq was Germany’s best-selling EV with 30,845 units, ahead of the Tesla Model Y (29,464) and the VW ID.3 (24,352).

The EV boom is happening during one of the worst years in the history of Germany’s auto industry.

In October, the VW brand’s German registrations fell 4%, Audi dropped 8.4%, Porsche lost 5.7%, and Opel crashed 24.1%. BMW was flat (+0.1%), and Mercedes was the exception, up 8.5%. VW is still by far the biggest brand in Germany with an 18.2% share, but it’s down 5.6% for the year.

Last week, Volkswagen Group reported a €5.9 billion operating loss for the third quarter, its biggest quarterly loss since Dieselgate, driven by a writedown of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and thin EV margins. The group has already approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs and close several German plants. Mercedes cut its 2026 car margin guidance to 2-3% last week, mainly because of China.

It’s not a product problem. VW’s new ID. Polo is sold out with over 30,000 orders, BMW has over 50,000 orders for the Neue Klasse iX3, and the Elroq leads the German EV market.

Germany is proving what we’ve been saying for years. Give buyers EVs they can actually afford, and they switch fast. Fully electric cars went from about 19% of the market last year to 37% in October, and the country beat the industry’s full-year forecast with two months to spare. That’s not a slow transition.

One thing to consider when talking about EVs not being Germany-made is that Germany car makers can't make them fast enough. A lot of the models are sold out for months. It's not an excuse but something to keep in mind.

Compare that with North America, where EV sales dropped 44% after the US killed its federal EV tax credit. Same technology, sometimes the same cars. The difference is policy.

Germany’s problem is who’s capturing the demand. Hint: it’s not German automakers.

But whose fault is that? You can’t spend years dragging your feet on electrification and lobby government back and forth on EV incentives and then complain when those who are all-in on EVs are able to take better advantage of the customer shift amid another oil crisis.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. #4641. Oldest evidence of cannabis use discovered in 2,700-year-old royal tomb

Published Nov 5, 2026 2:00 PM EST

The use of cannabis is documented across cultures stretching back thousands of years, but it frequently relates to harvesting the plant for hemp and other non-psychoactive products. That said, one Bronze Age society of horseriders living in present-day Russia called the Scythians may offer the oldest example of intentionally ingesting cannabis for its intoxicating properties. In the Eurasian steppes of Siberia, archaeologists have discovered a princely Scythian tomb complex featuring an estimated 1,000 cannabis seeds intentionally placed among the dead.

“The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial,” Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern in Switzerland, explained in a statement.

These weren’t simply symbolic objects, either. As Caspari and his colleagues detail in a study published today in the journal Science, human hair samples from the central burial room indicate Scythian royals also partook in cannabis use.

The Scythians were a group of ancient eastern Iranian nomadic equestrians renowned for their horseback skills. The community migrated from Central Asia into present-day Ukraine and southern Russia beginning in the eight and ninth centuries BCE, and stayed there for roughly the next 500 years. Their regional influence eventually waned before the Scythians ultimately assimilating into neighboring populations after being displaced by the Goths during the third century CE.

The burial complex Caspari’s team examined is located in Tuva, a south Siberian republic of Russia located along Mongolia’s northern border. Although ancient plant material like leaves, flowers, and resin generally decompose long before archaeologists can ever locate them, seeds sometimes endure when shielded from the elements. In this case, the royal tomb ensured near optimal conditions to protect the cannabis remnants. Laboratory radiocarbon dating of six recovered seeds indicate Bronze Age attendants likely placed them inside the burial chamber during the early eighth century BCE.

The exact details of Scythian cannabis cultivation and use remains unclear. Researchers theorize the plants were wild variants that naturally grew in the region. At the same time, hair analysis through methods like high-resolution mass spectrometry revealed the clear presence of cannabinol (CBN), which is produced by the oxidation of cannabis’ primary intoxicant, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). The team also noted weak signs consistent with THC itself.

The detection of these molecular signals doesn’t reveal how much cannabis the Scythian royals ingested, or the methods they used. At the same time, other Central Asian archaeological sites contained cannabinoid chemical remnants on heated stones and inside vessels, which strongly suggest inhalation.

“The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave, and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties,” concluded Caspari.

Archaeologists are now sequencing the DNA from some of the tomb’s seed samples, which will help them trace the plant’s spread and later human domestication. Cannabis wasn’t the only addition to the royal Scythian tomb, however. Prior work at the site has yielded the skeletal remnants of 18 horses arranged on the burial mound, along with an assortment of human bones.

“In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well,” added Caspari.

#4640. How do octopuses squeeze through tiny holes?

Published Nov 5, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Octopuses are famous for navigating their way through a tight squeeze. Even among invertebrates, their ability to compress themselves into seemingly impossibly tiny passageways is an impressive sight. But for years, marine biologists have remained perplexed by how these cephalopods routinely manage their maneuvers.

“There is no information about how octopuses squeeze through an opening far smaller than [their] body diameter,” Wenci Xin, a marine biologist at the National University of Singapore, said in a statement.

Xin and her colleagues recently provided Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) and young common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) with a chance to show off their skills. Their findings, published in a study today in the Journal of Experimental Biology, show that there may not necessarily be a “one size fits all” approach for octopuses.

First, the team needed some measurements. Previously, researchers assumed that an octopus’ stiff cranial case of cartilage that protects its central nervous system also dictates the limits of how small it can scrunch. Knowing this, Xin measured the distance between each specimen’s eyes to approximate the cartilage sheath’s width. In this case, the space between each octopus’ eyes ranged between about 0.6 and 1.3 inches wide.

The team then constructed customized, clear plastic aquarium boxes linked by holes either slightly larger or smaller than width between each set of octopus eyes. From there, they simply set up cameras, and let the cephalopods do their thing.

When encountering a comparatively large hole, each octopus initially prodded the opening with its arms before passing one limb through the hole. Usually, this was one of its two left front arms. It then slipped as many as five more arms through the portal, only to reach back with two of those limbs and use their suckers to stick to the initial box’s walls. Finally, they extended and stiffened these arms to push against the wall and maneuver the remaining limbs, mantle, and head through the hole. On average, an octopus successfully transitioned between boxes within about 20 seconds.

However, the octopuses often changed their approach when facing narrower holes often. The tighter squeeze limited how many arms an octopus could simultaneously thread through the opening. In these instances, the animals divided their final shimmying stage into two phases—first pulling all of its remaining arms through the hole, then compressing its mantle and scooting the rest of its body through the entry.

Well, only the common octopuses managed this. Xin’s team was surprised to learn the Mayan octopuses had no interest in the narrower holes. Instead, they simply hung out in another corner of the box without even testing the opening with their arms. Only when offered a second, larger passage did they get curious. In those scenarios, they felt around the smaller entry before opting to go through the larger of the two holes.

Although their study only focused on two species, their results indicate octopuses may vary in the ways they navigate tight spaces. At the same time, it appears their cranial cartilage may dictate at least some of their physical limitations. In any case, the biologists’ trials indicate that if an octopus at least thinks it can fit through an opening, it will certainly give it a try.

#4639. Range Rover is axing its two cheapest SUVs, making way for a new entry-level EV

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.

For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.

That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.

While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.

Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.

The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.

Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).

The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).

Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.

At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

#4638. When Grief Lies Just Below the Surface

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

In dealing with the recent passing of her grandmother, Aleh's reaction remained distanced, somehow removed. Yet when she dreamed of the death of an online acquaintance, and especially upon analyzing her dream, she was able to break through the disconnection and bring her feelings to the surface.

I met a woman last year, Autumn, who I communicate back and forth with online. Her brother Tobias passed away recently from health complications.

In this dream, I was excited to see her, since it had been so long and I felt the need to give her a big hug. I didn't get a chance to attend the funeral, so in my dreams, I told her I was so very sorry and that we will also miss him. It was a mixed feeling of happiness to see her, while also helping her grieve.

I wondered, "When did you have this dream?"

"Did you know Autumn's brother? It sounds like you did."

"No," Aleh said, "I didn't get the chance to meet him."

I added, "I'm curious about how you said you've known Autumn for a year but you 'communicate back and forth online.' You don’t see her in person?"

Aleh explained, "No, not anymore. We wanted to hang out, but with our busy schedules it’s been hard to plan anything. I've known Autumn for a year."

I suggested, "You mentioned that you had 'mixed feelings' in your dream. Can you think of a recent circumstance in your life you have 'mixed' feelings about, perhaps even a mix of happiness and grief?"

Aleh exclaimed, "My grandma passed away this past Sunday! I didn’t see her much the last few months because I knew it was coming. I've been a lot closer and communicating more with my parents. My dad's mom was the one who passed.

"I tend to remember more dreams after grief, it seems."

I said, "Perhaps Tobias’ appearance in your dream reflects your not seeing your grandmother in the months before she passed on. Why do you say you didn’t see her much 'because you knew it was coming'? Were you close with your dad’s mom?"

Aleh acknowledged, "I wasn't as close with her as I was with my grandpa growing up. I had a feeling it was almost time for her to pass away and wanted to keep her memory as someone very smiley and talkative. It didn't occur to me that Tobias appearing in the dream reflects me not seeing my grandmother. That really fits!"

I continued, "Let's investigate the two people who appear in your dream. Tell me, please, what comes to mind about Autumn's personality. What about Tobias? What do you know about him? Did you ever have a conversation with Tobias? Was he a friend too?"

Aleh offered, "Autumn is very happy. She has a great sense of humor and is always cracking jokes. I did have a conversation with Tobias online. He enjoyed conversations with many people online, giving motivational advice. He was also nice and very positive."

I reflected on Aleh's words. "Both your dream and your waking-life situation bring to mind matters involving death and funerals. Yet I'm struck by the light, happy tone of the words you're using: 'very smiley and talkative,' 'very happy,' 'motivational and positive.' You mentioned feeling a mix of happiness and grief, but I'm not hearing much grief.

"Does this observation ring true for you?"

Aleh responded, "I honestly didn't think about whether I've been feeling grief until you mentioned about my answers just now being pretty 'light.' I have to reflect on this. Now, I can also see that the characters in my dream aren't people I connect with on an everyday basis. They're nice, but I don't feel very connected to them."

I asked, "Does this lack of connection in your dream mirror any of your feelings in your waking-life situation?"

Aleh answered aloud and thoughtfully, "Am I really not grieving, or do I really not feel sad from my grandmother's passing? Am I so disconnected? No, I do feel sad, but what hurts me more is trying to be there for my parents. Especially my dad, who just lost his mom."

Making a clearer connection, she added, "Am I trying to comfort my own self in this dream? Omg I am, and I want to cry now. Finally."

The dream is Aleh's vehicle to comfort herself. In addition, by putting herself in a place where she's reaching out to someone who is grieving but who she feels less "connected" to than her own dad, she's giving herself some space to feel her own grief.

Additionally, we can see from this dream interpretation how important it is to pay attention to the words that the dreamer says when talking about all aspects of the analysis, not only while discussing the dream itself but also all associations with the dream. The precise words the dreamer uses during different parts of the discussion can often bring to the surface the emotional aspects of their waking-life situation that they are pushing below the surface.

#4636. Inside the persistent myth that giant pandas are bad at sex

Published Nov 5, 2026 5:00 PM EST

Excerpted from INTHE COMPANY OF PANDAS: My Life with the World’s Favorite Bear by Dr. Brandie Smith. Copyright 2026 © by Dr. Brandie Smith. Reprinted by permission of Atria Books, an Imprint of Simon & Schuster, LLC.

WHEN YOU take care of pandas, your primary responsibility is to make more pandas. I was told point-blank during my interviews to become curator, “Your job is to get the panda pregnant.” I had a PhD in population genetics, and while I’d picked up considerable experience with endangered-species reproduction at the theoretical level, my hands-on experience was limited. But nothing helps you adapt quickly to a new job like being asked to help the world’s most famous bear survive as a species.

When I arrived at the National Zoo, it had been almost three years since the birth of Mei Xiang and Tian Tian’s first cub, Tai Shan. There are usually two years between births, so the mood at the zoo was not worried, but determined. I was added to the weekly panda meeting, which included the curator, keepers, veterinarians, scientists, and even the zoo’s director—at the time I started it was John Berry, but segued to Dennis Kelly in 2010—as we pored over every detail of the breeding and birthing plans, making micro adjustments, to ensure not just a successful fertilization, but that Mei Xiang had everything an expectant panda mother needed to be happy. It was as if we could group-project a healthy cub into existence. And although I understood the intense desire to see a panda cub, I quickly learned the interest focuses not just on the offspring, but includes the reproductive act itself. And that level of detailed attention was not just for the panda professionals, but for the hobbyists as well. I think of pandas as being more adorable than alluring, but for some reason, a great many people are obsessed with their sex lives.

In 1972, when President Nixon contacted The Washington Star to share the news that Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing would be coming to the capital, he told the reporter, “The problem, however, with pandas is that they don’t know how to mate.” Director Ted Reed was aware of the “sex problem” and determined to get ahead of it. As part of the preparations for the pandas’ arrival, even though the pair were still too young to breed, he hired the zoo’s first female scientist, Devra Kleiman, as a reproductive zoologist. Over the years, he wrote frequently to Smithsonian Secretary S.Dillon Ripley about the zoo’s efforts to breed the animals and wryly acknowledged his unusual fixation. Reed saw the yearslong failure not just as his own (especially after optimistically promising baby pandas for the bicentennial year in 1976) but even more generally as a “defeat for machismo; an utter humiliation for all zoo males.” That these two very dignified men were sending letters back and forth in which the director referred to himself as the Smithsonian’s “resident sex maniac,” and, later, how he regretted that “the great panda sex orgy of 1979” had not materialized, was not at all inappropriate.

Talking about sex is necessary for the people responsible for breeding endangered species, especially when you’re talking about the important work of making more pandas. When it comes to pandas, it seems that everyone’s inhibitions fall away. Other species don’t get that pass. At the zoo, we see parents’ natural modesty kick in as they describe an elephant’s erection as an extra tail or leg, or they rush their children past a pair of amorous orangutans that are “just playing.” But when it comes to pandas, even if the animals are in the midst of attempting the act, a wide swath of the public, including families, will line up to watch and cheer them on.

Maybe it’s because they’re so cute that they seem more pure than prurient. I think most of our preoccupation with the sex lives of giant pandas derives from the urban legend that, when it comes to the basics of reproduction, these bears are completely clueless. This is demonstrably false because modern pandas, Ailuropoda melanoleuca, and their precursors have been on the planet for millions of years. In the wild, the panda lifespan is roughly fifteen to twenty years, so if you do the math, you can see that it took a lot of successful panda procreation to carry the species into the twenty-first century. So, where did this idea originate? And why does it persist?

In the Company of Pandas: Exploring the Secrets of the World’s Favorite Bear by Dr. Brandie Smith is available wherever books are sold on November 10.

Dr. Brandie Smith is the John and Adrienne Mars Director of the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute. With decades of experience in animal care, conservation, and zoo management, she has overseen critical breeding programs for endangered species and has personally witnessed some of the most dramatic moments in panda conservation history at one of America’s premier zoos. Originally from Indiana, Pennsylvania, she grew up around animals and began her professional career as an intern at the Pittsburgh Zoo and the National Zoo.

#4635. Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

“[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart said.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, said Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

“[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

Hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

“It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” said Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”

Bitner said women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

“[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she said. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”

In fact, Bitner said providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

Hart plans to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she said she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she said.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

“My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she said. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical company Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

“It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she said.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart said.

In everyday life, Bitner said that while some patients avoid talking about midlife issues like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

As more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep issues, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

“[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” said Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her issue because we know it’s not.”

#4634. Ford Fathom EV pickup prices will range from $28,350 to the high $30Ks

Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.

After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford said the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.

Even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”

The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.

Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley said, is perfect for today’s market.

The electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.

When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.

“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick said. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.

Frick said it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.

According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.

“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”

Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

I almost feel like the Fathom will be utilized similarly to how the Maverick is utilized and possibly become a big seller as well. It seems well suited for a small business work vehicle as well with fuel savings by going electric to add to the appeal.

The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also said the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

#4633. Hydroxyapatite toothpaste promises to better protect your teeth. Here’s what the science says.

Published Nov 6, 2026 8:49 AM EST

There’s a new kid on the block in the toothpaste aisle. Next to the usual fluoride formulas, another option has been appearing: hydroxyapatite toothpaste.

Hydroxyapatite is the same mineral found in tooth enamel, and some claim using hydroxyapatite toothpaste can help plug tiny cracks in your teeth. Many brands are touting the new toothpaste as an effective alternative to fluoride. But does it actually protect your teeth, or is it just another trendy wellness product? After speaking with several experts, it seems like hydroxyapatite toothpaste might be worth trying.

Hydroxyapatite is a mineral made mostly of calcium and phosphorus that naturally occurs in human bones and teeth. It’s the main mineral in tooth enamel, the hard outer coating that helps protect your teeth from damage.

“Enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, but it’s not invulnerable,” says Dr. Joachim Enax, a chemist and senior scientist at Dr. Kurt Wolff GmbH & Co. KG, which makes hydroxyapatite toothpastes. Acids from foods and from bacteria in the mouth can gradually dissolve minerals from the tooth surface. Toothpastes that contain hydroxyapatite are designed to put some of that mineral back and help repair very early enamel damage, Enax explains.

If you’ve looked at these products, you may have seen labels mentioning “nano-hydroxyapatite” or “micro-hydroxyapatite.” That refers to the size of the mineral particles in the toothpaste. “Nano crystals are very fine and microscopic. Micro-hydroxyapatite crystals are larger,” says Dr. Hardy Limeback, a professor emeritus in the faculty of dentistry at the University of Toronto, who has been critical of fluoride use.

Both nano- and micro-hydroxyapatite occur naturally—for example, in breast milk—and because they are chemically the same as the mineral in tooth enamel, “they are added to toothpaste to plug up micro cracks or etches on the tooth surface,” he explains.

Hydroxyapatite toothpaste is not actually new. In the 1960s, research at NASA on growing crystals for electronics led to a patent for repairing teeth by growing hydroxyapatite crystals. A Japanese company later acquired the patent and introduced the first hydroxyapatite-based toothpastes in the 1980s.

Since hydroxyapatite was approved as an anti-cavity ingredient in Japan in 1993, similar toothpastes have become available in Europe (since 2006) and Canada (since 2015).

In the United States, you can buy hydroxyapatite toothpastes online and in some stores, but neither the Food and Drug Administration nor the American Dental Association has approved hydroxyapatite as an anti-cavity ingredient. To earn the ADA’s Seal of Acceptance—an official indication that a toothpaste helps prevent cavities—a product must contain fluoride.

Hydroxyapatite toothpaste can help remineralize enamel that has been weakened by acids from dental plaque or acidic foods, say Limeback and Enax. By promoting remineralization and forming a protective layer that helps shield enamel from acids, it may also protect teeth against cavities, says Dr. Elżbieta Paszyńska, a dental surgeon and head of the department of integrated dentistry and endodontics at Poznan University of Medical Sciences in Poland.

Fluoride prevents cavities in a similar way: Fluoride ions are incorporated into the enamel’s structure, helping repair very early decay and making the enamel more resistant to acid over time.

Paszyńska’s group ran two randomized clinical trials at two medical universities, with nearly 200 participants each: one in children aged three to seven, and one in adults with healthy teeth. For 12 to 18 months, participants used either a hydroxyapatite or a fluoride toothpaste. (Both studies were funded by Dr. Kurt Wolff GmbH & Co. KG.)

“At the end of both studies, children and adults using the hydroxyapatite toothpaste were no more likely to develop new carious lesions than those using fluoride toothpaste,” she says. “These findings demonstrated, in two independent clinical trials, that hydroxyapatite toothpaste can provide caries [cavity] protection comparable to fluoride toothpaste in daily oral care.”

Hydroxyapatite toothpastes may also help reduce tooth sensitivity by physically filling and sealing exposed dentinal tubules (the tiny channels leading to tooth nerves), Limeback and Enax note. In one study, people who used a nano-hydroxyapatite toothpaste for two to four weeks were less sensitive to cold air and touch than they had been at the start.

Early studies—most conducted in laboratory settings—suggest that regular use of hydroxyapatite toothpastes can also have a whitening effect. The mineral can form a thin, white layer on the tooth surface that helps mask the yellow tones of the underlying dentin and reduce the appearance of stains.

“This is different from bleaching; it is about restoring and maintaining the natural appearance of enamel,” Enax says. But more clinical trials are needed to confirm this effect in people.

Why our ancestors had straight teeth without braces

Is crossing your eyes really bad for you? We asked an optometrist.

In Europe, health officials have closely studied nano-hydroxyapatite in toothpastes and mouthwashes. In July 2025, the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety said this ingredient is safe in amounts up to about 30 percent in toothpaste and 10 percent in mouthwash. Most products on the market use 10 percent or less, which is well within that limit.

In the studies they reviewed, rod-shaped nano-hydroxyapatite did not damage DNA or harm cells, even when tested at high concentrations on mouth tissue samples in the lab. (The safety opinion does not apply to products that use needle-shaped particles.)

The committee concluded that any tiny amount of nano-hydroxyapatite particles that enter the cells lining the mouth is naturally removed from the body when those cells shed. If you swallow some toothpaste by accident, the particles are expected to break down quickly in stomach acid, causing no harmful effects.

Even with growing evidence in its favor, some U.S. dentists are cautious about swapping fluoride for hydroxyapatite.

“As far as telling someone, ‘Hey, stop using fluoride toothpaste and start using this,’ we don’t have enough evidence yet,” Dr. Hema Arany, a dentist and associate professor at the Medical University of South Carolina, said in a recent interview. “And so when it comes to standard of care, we are not recommending hydroxyapatite toothpaste.”

But some people avoid fluoride because they’re worried about possible links between fluoride and skin problems or neurodevelopmental issues in children, though these concerns remain debated and the data is still evolving. The World Health Organization and the American Dental Association maintain that fluoride toothpaste is safe and highly effective at preventing tooth decay when used as directed.

According to ethical guidance published in the Journal of the American Dental Association, for people who refuse to use fluoride, hydroxyapatite “is likely the second-best option.”

#4632. GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

#4629. Inside Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center, which doles out 10,000 pounds of food every day

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Cases of peanut butter, bright red boxes of Shredded Wheat cereal, and so many varieties of tea that even Mary Poppins would be excited. Around the corner, large wooden crates teeming with wide leaves and sturdy grasses, and a walk-in refrigerator full of fresh produce sit ready to turn into dishes that are a feast for the eyes and the belly.

For the team working at Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center (ANC) at Walt Disney World Resort in Orlando, Florida, it’s like Thanksgiving every day. The roughly 40 cast members on the animal nutrition team is responsible for feeding the over 5,000 animals at Disney’s Animal Kingdom Theme Park and The Seas at EPCOT. It takes time, a devotion to the science of nutrition, and really knowing your audience to deliver about 10,000 pounds of food per day. And like putting together any big meal, it requires a team effort, which extends well beyond the animals at Disney.

“What we’re trying to do is provide the optimal nutrition for animals to live long and healthy lives, and we do that by taking information from a lot of different fields,” Animal Nutrition Operations Manager Dr. Heidi Bissell tells Popular Science. “From the field of agriculture, we learn a lot about animal physiology and how animals work, and can then design diets with the ingredients we have for specific purposes.”

In addition to bringing in knowledge from across different scientific disciplines, the team collaborates with other accredited zoos, aquariums, and universities to share research and data on animal nutrition. They’ve published studies on animals from bigger animals like zebras and rhinos, to smaller fish and amphibians, which is crucial to filling in nutritional gaps. If the team is not sure what a particular species needs to eat in order to thrive, they will turn to comparative nutrition for answers.

“We go with a close relative [and] take what we know about the animals we do know a lot about and apply that to some of our other species,” Bissell explains. “Then we learn from our own animals by assessing how they’re doing on the diets that we’re offering, so we can gauge their nutritional status and make adjustments as needed.”

Staying nimble and making these adjustments is also important. If a supply chain issue disrupts what the nutrition team can get, having a back-up plan that includes nutritious food is critical. If an animal is familiar and comfortable with at least a few types of food, they will generally fare better, whether there are shortages or not.

At the same time, the nutrition team works to ensure that the food and its presentation mimics life in the wild as much as possible.

“Animals in the wild are spending their days solving puzzles, trying to figure out how to eat, while staying away from predators or toxins,” Bissell says. “They’re making a lot of decisions all day, so if we just offered them food in a bowl that would not provide them with mental stimulation.”

One of the most common behaviors is foraging, or digging through obstacles like grass, mud, or leaves to find food. The dishes the team creates are often presented in a way that encourages foraging, so that the animals keep up those natural behaviors. Leaves will be hung up in a tree for the giraffes to eat as they would in the wild. Carnivores like lions will get whole prey and bones to eat, which also helps keep their own jaws and teeth healthy. The team also pays attention to seasonal shifts to keep animals in their natural rhythm.

“Probably the biggest group of animals that we do this with would be birds,” says Bissell. “If they’re laying eggs, they might need more calcium, so we might add sources of calcium into their diet.”

Surprisingly, feeding bigger animals like lions and elephants is not as challenging as making sure that the insectivores have enough to eat. True to their name, anteaters almost exclusively eat bugs, and can consume up to 3,000 insects per day. To keep up with all of those the bugs, Bissell and the team work side-by-side with manufacturers to ensure their insect pellets meet the physical and nutritional standards needed to align with insects the anteaters encounter in the wild. To supplement, the anteaters will also get a bit of produce with the insects, since they do also eat fruit.

“We do a lot with like ice cakes, where we can freeze food in blocks of ice and can color the water with like vegetable dyes, so it’s fun and engaging. And the ice, especially in Florida in the summer, is really nice for hydration,” Bissell explains. “We are often pulling from what’s already in the animal diet or similar things, because just like humans, it’s not a great idea to just add a bunch of stuff on top of your existing diet.”

They’ll also follow themes, from a little fall pies to a driver’s license out of fruit and leaves for a gorilla’s 16th birthday and a food sculpture shaped like a margarita for a 21st birthday. That devotion to keeping meals fresh and creative helps all animals, humans included.

“I like making animals’ lives better, and by extension people’s lives better, because we care about these animals so much,” says Bissell.

#4628. ‘Ferritin Face’: What Low Iron Actually Does (and Doesn't Do) to Your Appearance

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Social media influencers claim that having a “ferritin face” may indicate you’re low in iron.

Ferritin is a protein that helps your body store iron. You need iron in order to make healthy red blood cells, which carry oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. Iron is also important for bone marrow, organs, healthy muscles, and brain development.

As “ferritin face” makes its way across social media platforms, users are describing several tell-tale signs, including:

Users have also shared images of their face before and after taking iron supplements or getting an iron infusion. Videos about “ferritin face” have garnered millions of views on various platforms.

However, medical professionals state that your appearance alone is not enough to diagnose iron deficiency.

“It’s important to understand that ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis, nor is it a confirmed symptom of iron deficiency. While some people with iron deficiency can appear pale due to low hemoglobin levels in their red blood cells, there are many other symptoms to consider,” said Daniel Atkinson, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and clinical lead at Treated.

“Notably, these symptoms are also present in many different conditions, and their presence does not necessarily mean iron deficiency anemia or even low ferritin levels. Similar features are seen in people with iron processing and absorption issues, such as gluten intolerance, or in urgent sudden blood loss scenarios,” added Jonathan Jennings, MD, board certified internist at Medical Offices of Manhattan.

Iron deficiency can affect your skin and appearance. These signs are often subtle, but may include:

In some ways, the social media videos are correct. Your skin and face can change when your iron levels are low.

“The facial signs people point to, like pale skin and a washed-out look, mostly come from anaemia, when your haemoglobin has dropped. But iron deficiency and anaemia aren’t the same thing,” said Thom Phillips, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and Chief Medical Officer at Forth. “By the time low iron shows on your face, your stores are usually close to empty.”

It is important to speak with a healthcare professional, who will run blood tests such as a complete blood count and ferritin levels.

It is also important not to take iron supplements without first checking with your healthcare professional, because having too much iron in your body can also cause negative effects.

Too little and too much iron could raise your risk of infection, which is why it’s important not to take supplements without medical supervision.

The signs and symptoms of iron deficiency can depend on whether you are anemic or not. Some of the early signs may include:

“These symptoms typically occur because your body produces fewer red blood cells, which results in less oxygen being delivered throughout your body, making you feel tired and weak,” said Atkinson.

While your facial appearance can be a sign that something isn’t right, healthcare professionals consider other symptoms and how you feel overall.

They also rely on blood tests to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

“The misinformation is the idea that you can spot it yourself. That leads to two problems: people with low iron who look fine assume they’re OK, and people who look tired start taking iron supplements they don’t need,” said Phillips.

Atkinson also noted that factors such as different settings and environmental conditions can affect how your face appears.

That being said, the “ferritin face” trend may help bring awareness to certain symptoms and when to get them checked.

“[This] trend may raise some awareness about iron deficiency anemia and how low iron levels can impact daily life,” said Atkinson.

“Fatigue and lightheadedness are common side effects of low iron, but it manifests in other ways too, such as paler skin or increased hair shedding, which can be concerning for many people. If you experience these symptoms, you should let your doctor know so they can help treat the condition appropriately,” he said.

#4627. NASA teases experimental X-70 ‘Fractal’ aircraft

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:00 AM EST

NASA has unveiled its next experimental aircraft, dubbed the X-70 Fractal. Well, “unveiled” may be a bit of a stretch. During this week’s UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman announced plans for the “crewed, high-performance platform” designed to boost maneuverability, flight control, and “other cutting-edge technologies in real flight.”

Beyond that, you’re guess is probably about as good as anyone’s. Even X-70’s sole visual hint may mean nothing at all. The shadowy frame seen silhouetted by fog in NASA’s announcement is explicitly identified as AI “generated content.” This means even the rounded cockpit, splayed tail fins, and extended wings may ultimately not even show up in the final design.

Despite a lack of photographs, NASA did provide some more concrete details about the X-70. The aircraft will have a 10,000 pound takeoff weight and will cruise at Mach .75 (about 570 miles per hour) at a maximum altitude of 45,000 feet. Its operational range is also expected to exceed 1,500 nautical miles (1,726 miles).

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” NASA Research and Technology Mission Directorate director Laurie Grindle said in the agency’s announcement. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”

NASA also emphasized the X-70’s modular construction, which will allow quick swaps of internal and external payloads. As The War Zone noted, these features are likely intended to facilitate tests of experimental autonomous deployments and drone technology. The X-70 may also feature “bleeding-edge” abilities like morphing wings and “air-burst” controls, which allow aircraft to precisely maneuver midflight solely through blasts of pressurized air.

Isaacman said he expects the X-70 to complete its first flight within the next two years, although it’s always useful to take experimental aircraft timelines with a grain of salt. When NASA awarded Lockheed Martin the contract to develop its X-59 aircraft in 2016, the aim was to have a vehicle ready for testing by 2020. The actual X-59’s maiden flight ultimately took place on October 28, 2025.

#4626. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.
